talks.title: OffensiveCon19 - Attacking Hardware Root of Trust from UEFI Firmware
talks.teaser: 19 - Alex Matrosov - Attacking Hardware Root of Trust from UEFI Firmware.
talks.summary:
Alex Matrosov looks at how the hardware root of trust on modern x86 systems is often split between silicon and firmware, and how that split creates weak points. The main target is a Lenovo ThinkPad P50. The BIOS setup offers an option that appears to permanently disable the Computrace anti-theft component, but the talk shows that the setting is only a stored byte. Lenovo's Windows management interface reaches SMI handlers that let an administrator re-enable Computrace from the operating system without a kernel driver. The handler checks a one-byte secret, which the speaker brute-forced in under ten minutes on his own laptop.

The middle of the talk covers further findings. Lenovo's security configuration is kept in NVRAM variables, and the supervisor password prompt can be avoided on systems where no password is set, because the tries are counted. A platform configuration byte in an unprotected UEFI padding region can be changed to disable Boot Guard, which the speaker suggests is a manufacturing or recovery path. He also describes an embedded controller update flow where the vendor signs a SHA-256 hash but never checks the update payload against it, so a modified package with the same hash is accepted. A recovery path in one Intel-based firmware is another example, where a failed verification result did not stop the process.

The closing advice is to avoid trusting vendor claims about permanent disabling, to treat recovery and service features as attack surface, and to include firmware reverse engineering in threat models. The speaker argues that a root of trust handed off to software is only as strong as its weakest update or configuration path.

talks.title: OffensiveCon19 - Attacking Edge Through the JavaScript Just-In-Time compiler
talks.teaser: 19 - Bruno Keith - Attacking Edge Through the JavaScript Just-In-Time compiler.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how JavaScript engines work and why their just-in-time compilers are a rich source of memory corruption bugs. It opens with the open-source Chakra Core engine used by Microsoft Edge and the main parts of a typical engine, including the parser, bytecode interpreter, runtime and garbage collector. It then covers how Chakra encodes values with NaN boxing, and how objects separate their layout from their property values, which enables inline caching.

The middle of the talk walks through the JIT pipeline. The interpreter gathers profiling data, the compiler generates code that checks its assumptions, and failed checks lead to a slow path or a bailout. The forward pass of Chakra's global optimizer, along with its loop prepass, is the area of most interest for bugs. A worked example shows how a scalar object changes its internal layout when a fifth property is added, and how a compiler that fails to model this can skip a type check and overwrite the object's slot pointer.

The talk then turns that primitive into an exploit against a vulnerable build. Redirecting an ArrayBuffer's backing store gives arbitrary read and write through typed arrays. From there the exploit leaks a vtable pointer to find the engine's base address and a stack address, and it ends by running code in a demo. The takeaway is that JIT code must verify every assumption it makes, and that the same concepts apply to other JavaScript engines.

talks.title: OffensiveCon18 - Oh No, Where's FIDO?
talks.teaser: 18 - Markus Vervier and Michele Orru - Oh No, Where's FIDO?.

talks.title: 18 - Brian Gorenc, Abdul-Aziz Hariri and Jasiel Spelman
talks.teaser: Covers the VMware attack surface and three guest-to-host exploit case studies, ranging from a use-after-free to a stack bug.
talks.summary:
The talk starts by mapping the VMware Workstation and Fusion attack surface, where guest software crosses a trust boundary into the vmx host process. The speakers cover five areas: the always-on backdoor I/O channel, guest RPC handlers, SVGA 2D and 3D graphics, the XHCI USB controller, and virtual printing through a third-party print library. They show how to reach the backdoor from a guest, trace RPC requests with a Python debugger script, and call RPC functions from Python using ctypes. They also explain that comparing the debug build of vmx with the release binaries, and using open-source VMware tools headers and driver code, makes reversing easier.

The middle of the talk covers three exploitation case studies, ordered from simpler to much more complex. The first is a drag-and-drop use-after-free triggered by switching protocol versions, where a crafted RPC payload reclaims the freed memory and a ROP chain is pointed to from a global variable and moved onto a writable and executable region. The second is a heap overflow during drag-and-drop fragment reassembly, where repeated allocations shape the heap so that a drag-and-drop object leaks a base address. The third is an uninitialized stack variable in SVGA 3D handling, which is turned into repeated use-after-free and type confusion to leak heap and code pointers before control is redirected. The speakers note this bug was part of a larger browser-to-host chain.

The closing section argues that VMware has a large, under-researched attack surface and that its vulnerability-specific mitigations lag behind modern browsers. The speakers also describe how vendor duplicate checks revealed how little the vendor knew about its own code, and they encourage researchers to pursue these bugs.

talks.title: OffensiveCon18 - Robin Hood vs Cisco ASA AnyConnect
talks.teaser: 18 - Cedric Halbronn - Robin Hood vs Cisco ASA AnyConnect.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a vulnerability researcher at HCC Group, introduces Cisco ASA firewalls as widely used VPN gateways that run a single Linux-based binary with its own network stack. He explains how he found a pre-authentication bug by fuzzing the XML parser used by AnyConnect and clientless SSL VPN, using a simple template with mutated tags. He also walks through the patch timeline across ASA version branches, noting that fixes existed before the first advisory and that a later advisory widened the scope to other protocols that share the same parser.

The core of the talk is the root cause and the exploit. A dangling pointer left by one XML data handler leads to a double free of a 2000-byte chunk when a second crafted packet is sent. The exploit then uses IKEv1 IP fragment reassembly to shape the heap: creating holes, turning the double free into a repeatable free primitive, confusing a fragment length, and overflowing into adjacent chunks. Corrupting Cisco's mempool metadata yields a mirror write primitive, which the speaker uses to overwrite a function pointer and redirect execution to shellcode. The working demo targets an older 32-bit build without NX and without ASLR, and the speaker says newer releases would need a remote ASLR bypass.

For practitioners, the talk stresses that ASA branches live in parallel, so the right fix is the patched release on the branch in use rather than simply the highest version number. The speaker also shares the debugging and analysis tools his team released for firmware unpacking, GDB integration, heap inspection and IDA automation, and suggests that remote ASLR bypass and porting to 64-bit remain open next steps.

talks.title: OffensiveCon18 - Field Report on a Zero-Day Machine
talks.teaser: 18 - Niko Schmidt, Marco Bartoli, Fabian Yamaguchi - Field Report on a Zero-Day Machine.
talks.summary:
This talk gives a ten-year progress report on an effort to build a system that finds vulnerabilities in source code by capturing what human analysts know. The speakers argue that fuzzing works in practice because it lets an analyst mark an interface as attacker-controlled and treats a crash as a security-relevant violation. Classic static analysis lacks that link to analyst knowledge, so reports are full of code that turns out to be dead or unreachable.

To close that gap, the approach represents code as a semantic code property graph that combines syntax, control flow and data flow. Operators and library calls are reduced to function calls with summary edges, so code that has already been analysed does not need to be re-analysed. Analyst knowledge is stored in a small, non-Turing-complete rule language that defines sources, sinks, transformations and the flows that should or should not be reported. A query shell lets users explore the graph interactively and script queries from the command line.

The live demos ran on a sample Spring application, where request parameters were traced to a deserialisation-style read, on a parameter injection path that could alter a file path, and on a CSV injection in the OpenCMS content platform, where exported spreadsheet cells carried formulas. The takeaway is that encoding expert knowledge as reusable rules scales better than one-off queries. The speakers note that reflection remains hard for static analysis and needs case-by-case modelling.

talks.title: 18 - Ilya Smith
talks.teaser: Shows how Linux mmap placement and glibc loading make ASLR predictable, and proposes kernel and loader fixes.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how Linux address space layout randomization works on x86-64 and where it falls short, focusing on the kernel's mmap placement and the GNU C library loader. Starting from a process memory map, the speaker shows that shared libraries are packed next to each other and loaded in a fixed order. A single leaked pointer, or an out-of-bounds read or write, can therefore reveal the offsets of other regions, and distribution packages make those offsets easy to compute.

Several weaknesses were presented. Gaps left by ELF segment handling can hold allocations near the main thread's TLS block, which holds the stack canary, and new thread stacks sit close to the libraries, so a small overwrite can reach the canary. glibc's aligned mmap for new heaps leaves little randomness, and freed stacks and heap chunks are cached and reused, so a leaked address stays useful. The loader also does not validate ELF program header order, letting a crafted file remap libc, and a kernel check against mmap_min_addr that assumes a hardcoded page size can cause permission errors and denial of service when the sysctl is raised.

The speaker proposed fixes: reserving unmapped holes with PROT_NONE, validating segment order in the loader, separating stack canaries from the stack, and choosing random free gaps in the kernel's mmap search. A kernel prototype was tested on a recent Ubuntu release, with added search overhead and limits to 64-bit systems. The takeaway is that predictable region placement turns small leaks into full layout disclosure, so defenders should treat loader and mapping behaviour as part of the exploit surface.

talks.title: 18 - Rodrigo Branco - Inside the Machine
talks.teaser: Argues that mitigations should be proven against real exploits and that offensive research should drive defensive investment.
talks.summary:
The keynote challenges how the industry talks about mitigations. Vendors often say a defense "raises the bar" without saying against whom, in which scenarios, or by how much, and the maintenance cost of a mitigation is rarely weighed when it is proposed or revisited in later product generations. The speaker suggests a baseline: a proposed mitigation should fully stop at least three real vulnerabilities before it is accepted.

The talk then argues that people who propose mitigations need to understand exploitation. Conference presentations usually show a successful technique and leave out failed attempts, non-exploitable cases and the engineering work behind a working exploit, so watching one exploit does not give that understanding. The speaker points to language-theoretic security, which favors validating input at the point it enters a program, as conflicting with common secure development advice to check input close to where it is used. Academic work on formalizing heap exploitation and on the theory of why exploits are possible is presented as a way to model mitigations mathematically. Microsoft buying exploits to inform mitigations and the academic naming of ROP after practitioners had used the technique are offered as examples.

The closing argument is that defensive investment should be led by offensive researchers rather than by architects who lack that depth. The speaker said a forthcoming paper will use set theory to model exploits and mitigations, so practitioners can reason about both more rigorously.

talks.title: OffensiveCon18 - New and Improved UMCI, Same Old Bugs
talks.teaser: 18 - James Forshaw - New and Improved UMCI, Same Old Bugs.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits User Mode Code Integrity (UMCI), a Windows allowlisting feature introduced in Windows 8 and used on Windows RT and Windows 10 S. The kernel checks signatures against a policy file, and enlightened script engines such as PowerShell receive extra restrictions. The speaker's goal was arbitrary code execution without admin rights, using only built-in components.

The first route used a compiled HTML help file, which runs in the local machine zone, but COM object creation was blocked there. Examining how the check worked showed that class IDs were compared against a short hard-coded allowlist before CoCreateInstance ran. Per-user Treat As registry links let an allowed class ID resolve to a banned one. The registry editors were blocked, so the built-in regini.exe tool wrote the keys instead. An HTML object tag then supplied the allowed class ID directly, which gave .NET code execution and then PowerShell. A second bypass targeted cached image signatures. Requesting one mode of the cache signing call needs no protected process, and a window existed between hashing a file and writing the cache attribute in which the file could still change. That let an unsigned copy of Process Explorer run.

The speaker judged most goals met, though drop-and-run still needed user clicks. Later builds such as 1709 blocked more binaries, but a demo on an updated system still showed one route working, with details left for public references. The takeaway is that an allowlist is only as strong as every step that resolves and verifies a component, especially when the check and the use happen at different times.

talks.teaser: 18 - Joe Bialek - The Evolution of CFI Attacks and Defenses.

talks.title: 18 - Jos Wetzels and Ali Abbasi
talks.teaser: Analyzes QNX 6 and 7 random number generators and exploit mitigations, finding weak entropy and broken defaults.
talks.summary:
The talk examines QNX, a POSIX-style real-time microkernel operating system used in automotive infotainment, network routers and industrial and medical devices. Since QNX is closed source, the researchers worked from reverse engineering. They outline its attack surface, including local services, remote network services and a history of setuid and permission bugs, then focus on the random number generators and exploit mitigations of QNX 6 and 7.

QNX 6 seeded its user-space generator from weak boot-time values and never fed runtime entropy back in, while the Fortuna-based redesign in QNX 7 still depends on weak runtime sources. QNX 6 ASLR offered about 4.5 bits of min-entropy, and a demo service was brute-forced to a root shell in seconds. Stack canaries averaged under eight bits, the stack stayed executable unless a startup flag was set, and the RELRO fix in 6.6 left the global offset table writable. Information leaks and QNET's trust of user IDs rounded out the findings.

Many issues were fixed in QNX 7 and patched in 6.6, but embedded update cycles mean flawed devices will stay in the field for years. The takeaway for practitioners is to check startup flags, entropy sources and integration choices on any QNX firmware they assess.

talks.title: 18 - Jörn Schneeweisz
talks.teaser: Gives a tongue-in-cheek critique of the security industry, from persistent bugs to layered abstractions and rising software complexity.
talks.summary:
The talk was an unscripted rant given in an opening slot after a scheduled keynote speaker could not attend. The speaker argues that the industry mostly patches individual holes instead of fixing root causes. Old bug classes such as cross-site scripting, SQL injection and memory corruption still turn up, and eliminating one of them would upset the bounty economy.

Several examples support the argument. The speaker describes finding application secrets committed to GitHub and a disclosed flaw in an ISP customer management panel, where a follow-up check of session cookies suggested only about 80 percent of installations had been patched. Mitigations such as non-executable memory are portrayed as making exploitation harder rather than solving it, and antivirus software as adding its own attack surface. Layered abstractions, from compilers removing security checks to modern software growing with Moore's law, are contrasted with a Commodore 64 that one user could understand fully.

The closing section contrasts the lenient input-handling principle, often called Postel's law, with the strict parsing approach of LangSec, noting that developers often pick leniency to meet deadlines. The speaker sees no easy fix such as starting from scratch, since people will not abandon their devices. The takeaway is modest: treat abstractions as hiding risk, treat mitigations as partial, and expect these problems to persist.
